    • Environment: Cold is a requirement, not a hardship: the plant needs a real winter — roughly 1,000 to 2,500 hours of cold between freezing and about 45 °F (7 °C) — to set its flower buds properly, which is why it belongs to the cool north (about USDA zones 2–7)
    • Planter or ground: Ground in a built bed of peat and sand, or a large container of the same mix — a home bed never needs a bog
    • Water: Constant moisture — about an inch of water a week, the bed kept moist like a wrung sponge — but the vines are not under water while they grow: growers flood a bed only in winter, to wrap the vines against killing cold, briefly in spring, to shield blossom buds from a late frost, and at harvest
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens from mid-September into November, deep red and firm — and ripe cranberries bounce, because each berry carries small pockets of air inside it; at home, pick by hand when the colour is full; sound fresh berries keep for weeks in the fridge and freeze exactly as they are

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: an evergreen trailing perennial of the heath family — a true kin of the blueberry it shares its family section with. Wiry runners run 1–6 ft (0.3–1.8 m) along the ground and root as they go; from them rise short upright stems, only a few inches tall, that carry the flowers and fruit. The whole plant stays under about 8 inches (20 cm) high and spreads into a dense, glossy mat. A planting is nearly permanent: vines live for decades, and some commercial beds planted in the 1800s are still cropping.
    • Sanding: every few years, spread a thin layer of clean sand over the bed, as Hall found by accident in 1816. The sand roots the runners, holds back weeds, and buries some pests and diseased leaves. It is the oldest trick in cranberry growing because it still works.
    • Commercial growers pick two ways: dry harvest, raking the berries off with scoops for the fresh market, and wet harvest, the famous one — the bed is flooded until the water covers the vines, machines knock the berries loose, and the floating fruit is corralled on the surface and lifted out, bound for juice and sauce. A home bed never needs flooding to pick.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2018) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: cranberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Williams et al. (2023) — Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews — 50 trials, 8,857 people; who benefits and who does not
    • National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (2024) — Cranberry: usefulness and safety — prevention not treatment; the warfarin question; food amounts in pregnancy
    • U.S. Food and Drug Administration (2020) — Letter of enforcement discretion: qualified health claims for cranberry juice beverages and cranberry dietary supplements — "limited" and "limited and inconsistent"
    • Cape Cod Cranberry Growers' Association — the history of cranberries in Massachusetts — Wampanoag use, the craneberry name, Hall's 1816 sanding

    Elderberry

    Sambucus nigra

    CulinaryMedicinal

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCookedDried

    BerryFlowerBarkLeaf

    The elder is a hedgerow shrub — in Europe it can grow into a small tree — that gives two harvests a year. In early summer it covers itself in flat plates of creamy, sweet-scented flowers; by late summer those plates have become heavy, drooping clusters of small purple-black berries. Both harvests are food, and both are medicine in the old records. But this plant has a rule, and it comes before everything else on this page: the berries are eaten cooked, never raw. Raw or unripe elderberries — and the leaves, bark, stems and roots in any form — carry cyanide-making compounds and gut-irritating proteins that bring on nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhoea. Cooking destroys them, which is why every traditional preparation in this entry, from syrup to jam to wine, heats the fruit. Follow that rule and the elder is generous; ignore it and the elder bites.

    Varieties

    • This entry holds two elders, and the varieties split by homeland. The European elder (S. nigra) grows into a large shrub or small tree, commonly to about 20 ft (6 m). The American elder (subsp. canadensis) is a smaller, suckering shrub of 5–12 ft (1.5–3.6 m) that spreads into a thicket, and it is the hardier of the two. Their berries are used the same way, under the same cooking rule.
    • Adams (American) — the old standard, released in 1926 and still planted: vigorous, productive, the benchmark the newer varieties are measured against.
    • York (American) — among the largest berries of any elder, ripening late; pair it with an earlier variety so the two flower together and crop well.
    • Nova (American) — an early-ripening, heavy-bearing variety, a natural partner for York.
    • Bob Gordon (American) — a 2011 release, selected from a wild plant found near Osceola, Missouri. Among the sweetest elderberries grown, with heavy crops on drooping heads that hang face-down — which the birds find harder to strip.
    • Wyldewood (American) — released in 2010 by the University of Missouri, with extra-large flower heads; a first choice where the flowers are harvested as well as the fruit.
    • Ranch (American) — a tough, upright grower that tolerates poorer ground and wind better than most.
    • Haschberg (European) — Austria's orchard elder, the backbone of the European elderberry juice trade: large clusters of dark, juice-rich berries on a vigorous tree.
    • Samdal and Sampo (European) — Danish selections bred for the juice crop, heavy-bearing and grown commercially in northern Europe.
    • Black Lace and Black Beauty (European) — the garden elders: deep purple, almost black foliage (finely cut, like lace, in Black Lace) with pink flowers. They fruit like any elder, but they are planted for their looks — the elder as an ornamental, which is why the class is honestly available to this entry even though the cap gives it to the three above.

    Around the World

    Britain — the hedgerow elder. Elderflower cordial and elderberry wine are the twin drinks of the British summer and autumn, and Pontack sauce is the old keeper: a sharp sauce of elderberries, vinegar and spice, named for Pontack's Head, a London tavern of the late 1600s, made to be laid down for years and used as a ketchup on meat and fish.
    Germany and Austria — Holunder country. Austria grows Haschberg in orchards; much of the European crop goes to juice, and the berry's dark pigment is used to colour other foods. In early summer the flowers are dipped in batter and fried as fritters — Hollerküchle — and elderflower syrup stands in every kitchen.
    Scandinavia — elderflower cordial (Danish hyldeblomstsaft, Swedish fläderblomssaft) is the taste of early summer, drunk diluted all season. This is also the Elder Mother's home ground, where the asking-before-cutting custom was strongest.
    Hungary — bodza: elderflower syrup (bodzaszörp) is a standard home-made drink, and the berries go into jams and the fruit soups of the region.
    North America — the American elder's country: elderberry pie, jelly and wine from farm kitchens, a small and growing Midwest farm crop (the Missouri breeding work behind Bob Gordon and Wyldewood), and behind all of it the far older Indigenous use of the plant.

    Where It Comes From

    • The elder is native across Europe, North Africa and western Asia, growing in hedgerows, wood edges and waste ground wherever the soil is rich and damp. North America has its own branch of the same species — the American elder, Sambucus nigra subsp. canadensis — a suckering shrub of the eastern half of the continent. This entry covers both: the same plant in two homelands, with the same rule about cooking.
    • The names are old. Sambucus comes from the Greek sambuca, a harp-like instrument the Romans knew; Pliny used the name nearly two thousand years ago. "Elder" itself is traced to the Anglo-Saxon æld, fire — because the plant's hollow stems, their soft pith pushed out, were used as blowpipes to kindle a fire. The same hollow stems gave it the country names Pipe Tree and Bore Tree.
    • Few plants were used for so much. Flowers, berries, bark, leaves and root all stood in the old herbals, and the elder was called the medicine chest of the country people. The writer John Evelyn put it in 1664: if the medicinal properties of elder's leaves, bark and berries were fully known, there was hardly an ailment for which a countryman could not fetch a remedy from every hedge. Those uses are history, told here as history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • In Denmark, the tree was held to be lived in. The Elder Mother — Hyldemoer, in the old Danish — dwelt in the elder, and no one cut the tree or took its wood without asking her leave first. A cradle made from elder wood was said to bring her anger down on the child lying in it. Hans Christian Andersen put her into a story of his own, "The Elder-Tree Mother" (1845), in which she rises from a pot of elderflower tea and shows a sick boy the whole of his life in the flowers. An elder growing by the house — by the back door, people said — was held to guard the home.
    • The same tree carried darker stories. Legend said that Judas hanged himself from an elder, and elder was one of the trees accused of giving the wood for the Cross. Its wood was not burned on the fire: people said it spat and screamed as it burned, and that burning it brought ill luck. And to stand beneath an elder on Midsummer's Eve, it was said, was to see the King of the Fairies ride past with his court.
    • In North America, the Indigenous peoples of the continent had their own long knowledge of their elder: the berries cooked for food, the flowers and other parts in their medicine, centuries before Europeans arrived. Settlers took the plant up, and elderberry pie, jelly and wine became staples of the American country kitchen.
    • The medicine tradition ran on two tracks that this page keeps apart. The berry became syrup — elderberry syrup stood in an official British pharmacopoeia of 1788, listed for coughs, colds and constipation — and syrup is what the modern flu trials tested. The flower became tea, the old sweating tea for a cold, and dried elder flower is the part Europe's herbal regulators accept today. Berry and flower have separate records, and neither one's record is borrowed for the other.

    Craft

    • The hollow stems were craft as much as story. With the pith pushed out, a length of elder stem became a pipe, a whistle, a flute or a boy's pop-gun — Culpeper joked that every boy with a pop-gun knew the elder tree. Pliny recorded the country belief that the shrillest pipes were cut from elders growing out of earshot of a cock's crow. The hard wood beneath the pith was worked into pegs, spindles and combs, and the berries, bark and leaves all gave dyes — purple, black and green.
    • What is in the berry: per 100 g of ripe raw berries — 73 kcal, carbohydrate 18.4 g, fibre 7.0 g, protein 0.66 g. The standout nutrient is vitamin C at 36 mg, about 40% of the daily value, with potassium at 280 mg, a little iron (1.6 mg) and vitamin B6 besides. Two honest notes: those figures are for the raw berry, and cooking — which is not optional — costs some of the vitamin C, though the fibre stays; and a syrup's sweetness is the maker's sugar, not the berry's. The deep purple-black colour is anthocyanins, plant pigments that behave as antioxidants in laboratory tests; that is chemistry, stated as chemistry, not a promise.
    • Flu — the claim this plant is famous for, and its full record. In 1995, during an outbreak of influenza B in an Israeli farming community, 27 people were given either a standardised elderberry syrup (sold as Sambucol) or a dummy syrup: nearly 90% of the elderberry group were well within two to three days, while the dummy group took at least six. In 2004, a Norwegian trial of 60 people with influenza A or B, run the same way, found symptoms easing on average four days earlier on the syrup, with less use of other medicine. A 2009 trial of elderberry lozenges in 64 people pointed the same way. Gathered together in a 2019 meta-analysis (Hawkins et al.), the four trials held only 180 people in total, and the reviewers found that elderberry substantially shortened and softened upper-respiratory symptoms — the effect clear for flu, and resting on a single trial for the common cold.
    • The other side of the record, at the same size. In 2020 an independent American trial (Macknin et al.) gave 87 people aged five and up, all with laboratory-confirmed flu, the same syrup at the same dose as the 2004 trial — and found no benefit at all: symptoms lasted the same on elderberry as on the dummy syrup. One after-the-fact analysis hinted that those on elderberry without the flu drug oseltamivir did slightly worse; it was an unplanned analysis, and the authors drew no firm conclusion from it. The honest summary of the whole record: several small early trials said yes, the largest independent trial said no, and the question is still open.
    • The funding is part of the record too. The positive flu trials tested one company's syrup, and that syrup's developer was among the researchers behind them; the air-traveller trial below used a commercial extract with its maker's support. That does not make the results false — it is context a reader is owed, and it is why the independent 2020 trial matters.
    • Colds and prevention. In a 2016 trial (Tiralongo et al.), 312 long-haul air travellers took elderberry capsules around their flights. They caught colds at the same rate as the group on dummy capsules — elderberry did not prevent colds — but those who did catch one had a shorter, milder illness. Nothing in the record shows elderberry preventing flu either, and it is not a substitute for the flu vaccine. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health puts it plainly: some preliminary research suggests elderberry may relieve symptoms of flu and colds; there is not enough good evidence to recommend it.
    • COVID-19, both directions handled plainly. Elderberry was promoted for COVID-19; there is no good evidence it helps, and US regulators took action against companies that claimed it did. The opposite fear — that elderberry might over-stir the immune system into a dangerous "cytokine storm" — rests on one laboratory finding, in which the syrup raised immune signalling chemicals in blood cells in a dish. A 2021 review of the human evidence (Wieland et al.) found no sign of that overstimulation in people. Neither the hope nor the fear has been shown in people, and this page claims neither.
    • The flower's own standing. Dried elder flower, taken as a tea, is accepted by the European Medicines Agency for the relief of early symptoms of the common cold — as a traditional use. That phrase has a precise meaning: the acceptance rests on the flower's long, documented history of use, and the agency's committee noted the lack of clinical trials behind it. It is a standing the berry does not hold, and the berry's trials do not transfer to the flower.
    • Safety — the part of this page that matters most. Cook the berries, and eat nothing else of this plant. The cyanide-making compound is chiefly one called sambunigrin, and it is not spread evenly: measured amounts run highest in the leaves and in green, unripe berries, far lower in the ripe fruit, and lowest of all in the flowers — which is one reason the flowers have their own gentler tradition. Strip ripe berries from their stalks before cooking, because the stalks carry more of it than the fruit. Heat destroys both the cyanide-makers and the lectins, the gut-irritating proteins the raw plant also holds.
    • The documented case. In August 1983, at a gathering in Monterey County, California, wild elderberries were pressed raw for juice with their leaves and branches crushed in. Of the 25 people there, 11 fell ill within minutes — nausea and vomiting — and eight were flown to hospital by helicopter; one was kept in, and all recovered. The US Centers for Disease Control reported the case in 1984, and its advice stands as this page's rule: the berries may be safe, particularly cooked; leaves and stems must never be crushed in.
    • The American berry, measured. Modern laboratory analysis of the American subspecies found its cyanide-making compounds low in every part of the plant, and none measurable in commercial juice — the ripe American berry sits at the mild end of its family. The rule stands anyway, for both subspecies: ripe, stripped from the stalks, and cooked.
    • Know the plant before you pick it. Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus), a knee-high, non-woody relative, carries more poisonous berries and is never food. In North America, pokeweed's dark berries grow on a tall plant with thick magenta stems — a different plant entirely, and a dangerous confusion. If you are not certain of the plant, do not pick.
    • Pregnancy and breastfeeding: little is known about elderberry's safety in either, so medicinal use is best left alone. Anyone taking regular medicine — above all medicines that damp down the immune system — should talk to their clinician before using elderberry products.
    • When to plant: Plant two different varieties growing near each other — within about 60 ft (18 m) — because elder is only partly self-fruitful and two kinds flowering together set far heavier crops; space American plants about 6 ft (1.8 m) apart and let the thicket form
    • Sun: Full sun gives the best fruit; part shade is tolerated
    • Soil: Moist, fertile, well-drained ground, mildly acid to neutral (about pH 5.5–6.5); the American elder in particular will grow in damp ground that defeats other fruit
    • Environment: The American elder is hardy in zones 3–9; the European in about zones 4–7
    • Planter or ground: Ground: the American elder makes a multi-stemmed thicket 5–12 ft (1.5–3.6 m) tall and spreads by suckers — new stems rising from the roots — so give it a corner it can own; the European elder grows larger, into a small tree of about 20 ft (6 m)
    • Water: Keep young plants watered in their first years; settled plants are tough
    • When to pick: Flowers: pick whole heads on a dry morning, just as they fully open, and use them the same day for cordial or fritters, or dry them for tea. Berries: pick a cluster only when every berry on it is fully dark — purple-black and soft — and the head hangs heavy; clip whole clusters, strip the berries off with a fork or your fingers, pick out any green berries and bits of stalk, and cook the berries before eating them, always

    Garden notes

    • A deciduous, fast-growing plant that asks for little. Both flower in flat, creamy plates — May to June in Europe, June into July in North America — and the berries ripen from late summer, roughly August to September. A settled bush yields roughly 3–15 lb (1.4–6.8 kg) of berries in a season.
    • Pruning is simple and forgiving. Fruit comes on young canes. Each winter, cut out dead wood and any cane older than three years, and keep the strongest young canes standing. Or take the renovation route: cut the whole plant nearly to the ground every few years and let it regrow — it fruits on the new growth.
    • New plants are easy: push hardwood cuttings into the ground in winter and most will root, or dig up a sucker and move it.
    • Birds love the ripe fruit and will strip a bush in days; net the plant, or pick promptly, or plant enough to share. Every flower head picked is a berry cluster given up, so pick a share and leave the rest.

    Mulberry

    Morus spp.

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCookedDried

    FruitLeafBarkWood

    A mulberry is not one fruit but a crowd. Each berry-shaped cluster is dozens of tiny fruits joined together — every bump on it was once a single flower — and it ripens soft, sweet and so full of dark juice that it stains fingers, tongues and pavements on contact. Three species share the name: the white mulberry of China, grown for five thousand years as the one food of the silkworm; the black mulberry of Persia, grown for the fruit itself and the richest-flavoured of the three; and the red mulberry, North America's own. Between them they fed an industry that dressed emperors and bankrupted speculators — and the fruit was almost a by-product.

    Varieties

    • The library treats the three species as this entry's varieties, because with mulberries the species is the choice that matters — each is a different tree with a different home, habit and fruit.
    • White mulberry — Morus alba — the silkworm tree of China, and now the most planted mulberry on earth. A fast-growing, tough tree of 30–50 ft (9–15 m). The fruit is ½–1 in (1.5–2.5 cm) long, ripening white, pink, red or purple-black by variety, sweet and mild — beside the black mulberry, often called plain. Named forms: 'Tehama', a California selection with large white fruit; 'Pakistan', whose fruit runs several inches long, kin to the long-fruited Himalayan mulberry; 'Pendula', a weeping form grown purely for looks; and the fruitless males, planted by the thousand as shade trees in dry cities — all leaf and pollen, no fruit at all.
    • Black mulberry — Morus nigra — the fruit tree of Persia and the Mediterranean, and the connoisseur's mulberry. A slow-growing, wide-spreading tree of 20–30 ft (6–9 m) that can live for centuries and grows gnarled and hollow with age. The fruit is about 1 in (2.5 cm) long, dark purple-black, with deep red juice and the richest flavour of the three — sweet and sharp together, and only fully itself when completely ripe; an under-ripe black mulberry is sour enough to pucker. It ripens late: midsummer, and into September in cool districts.
    • Red mulberry — Morus rubra — North America's own, a woodland understorey tree of 35–50 ft (10–15 m) with large, rough, hairy leaves. The fruit ripens dark red to black and tastes between the white and the black — sweet with some bite. It is now the rarest of the three in the wild: in Canada it is listed as endangered, with only a few hundred wild trees known, and across its range it is being crossed out of existence by its own cousin (told below).
    • 'Illinois Everbearing' — the backyard favourite of cold-winter country: an American selection, a cross between the white and red mulberries, hardy and heavy-cropping, with dark, flavourful fruit that ripens a few at a time from early summer well into autumn instead of all at once. For a home garden in a cold district it is the usual recommendation, and the long season is the reason.
    • Telling the three apart, in the hand: white mulberry leaves are smooth and somewhat glossy; red mulberry leaves are rough and hairy, like fine sandpaper; black mulberry leaves are rough with short, stiff hairs and sit on very short stalks, the fruit hugging the branch. Fruit colour alone will not tell you — all three can ripen dark.

    Around the World

    China — the homeland of the white mulberry and of silk: five thousand years of planting the tree for its leaves, with the fruit eaten fresh and dried, the leaf drunk as tea, and every part of the tree in the old medicine books.
    Japan — China's great silk rival in its day, when raw silk was among Japan's top exports and mulberry fields covered whole districts. The sericulture has shrunk; the leaf tea, kuwa-cha, is still drunk.
    Turkey — white mulberry country. The harvest is shaken down in early summer and boiled into dut pekmezi, a thick, dark mulberry molasses second only to grape pekmez among Turkey's fruit syrups, eaten at breakfast with tahini; the rest is dried into pale, raisin-sweet dut kurusu, sold in every market, or spread into pestil, a sun-dried fruit leather. Anatolia's villages are full of the trees.
    Iran — toot: dried white mulberries kept in a bowl beside the tea, nibbled in place of sugar cubes, as they have been for centuries. The black mulberry is shah toot, "the king's mulberry," eaten fresh in its short season and prized above the white for flavour.
    Central Asia — along the old Silk Road the dried fruit was travel food and winter food at once: light, sweet, keeping for months without spoiling. In high valleys such as Hunza, dried mulberries were a staple of the winter store, even ground into a sweet flour.
    India — the other great silk land: the mulberry fields of Karnataka, in the south, feed silkworms to this day, and India remains one of the world's two great silk producers. The fruit is eaten in the north, where black mulberries are a brief summer pleasure.
    England — the black mulberry as a garden monument: gnarled veterans stand in the grounds of old houses, colleges and rectories, some of them planted in James I's era or grown from those that were. The garden of Buckingham Palace, on the ground of the king's own mulberry plantation, now holds the national collection of mulberries.
    United States — two mulberries at once: the native red, foraged for pies, jam and eating out of hand wherever it still grows wild; and the escaped white, bird-sown along every fencerow, feeding birds and staining sidewalks from coast to coast — plus its fruitless male form, the shade tree of the desert Southwest, whose other side is told in the garden notes below.

    Where It Comes From

    • Three trees, three homes. The white mulberry (Morus alba) comes from China. The black mulberry (Morus nigra) comes from south-western Asia, most likely the highlands around Iran, the Caucasus and Armenia, though it has been planted for so long that its wild home is guesswork. The red mulberry (Morus rubra) is native to eastern North America, from Ontario and Minnesota down to Florida and Texas. All three belong to the fig family, Moraceae — kin to figs, jackfruit and breadfruit.
    • The Latin names are simply the colours: alba white, nigra black, rubra red. They mislead a little. The names record the fruit of the kind first described, not of every tree — a "white" mulberry's fruit can ripen white, pink, red or purple-black, and plenty of white mulberries bear dark fruit. The species tells you the tree's home and habits, not always the colour in the bowl.
    • Like the pineapple, the mulberry fruit is a multiple fruit: a whole spike of tiny flowers swells and fuses into one cluster. That is why it looks like a blackberry but has no core and no single berry's structure — and why it is so soft. There is almost nothing holding it together, which is also why it cannot be shipped fresh and is so rarely sold.
    • The silk story begins in China more than five thousand years ago — silk cloth survives from Neolithic sites there. The story China told about its discovery is this: the Empress Leizu, wife of the Yellow Emperor, was drinking tea beneath a mulberry tree when a silkworm cocoon fell into her cup. In the hot tea the cocoon loosened into a single shining thread, and she saw that it could be wound and woven. She is remembered as the Silkworm Mother. It is a story, told as a story — but the tree at its centre is real, and so is what the story explains.
    • The silkworm, Bombyx mori, is a moth caterpillar that eats mulberry leaves and, in practice, nothing else — and it does best on the white mulberry above all. One cocoon is a single thread hundreds of metres long. So wherever silk was wanted, white mulberries were planted: the tree and the worm travelled together, west along the roads that took silk's name, the Silk Road. For thousands of years China guarded the secret of how silk was made, and the cloth travelled without the knowledge.
    • The knowledge escaped around 550 CE — by the account the Byzantine historian Procopius told, two monks who had lived in the silk country hid silkworm eggs in their hollow bamboo canes and carried them to the Emperor Justinian in Constantinople. Historians doubt eggs could have survived the journey; what is certain is that silk-making reached the Byzantine world in that era, and the white mulberry came with it, then spread through the Mediterranean and into Italy, France and Spain as the food of Europe's silk industries.
    • Rome gave the fruit its most famous story. In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Pyramus and Thisbe, lovers in Babylon kept apart by their families, arranged to meet at night under a white mulberry tree. Thisbe fled a lioness; Pyramus, finding her bloodied veil, believed her dead and killed himself beneath the tree, and Thisbe, returning, did the same. Their blood soaked the roots, and the mulberry's fruit, white before, turned dark red — which is why, the story says, ripe mulberries carry the colour of blood. Shakespeare retold it as the bungled play inside A Midsummer Night's Dream. A mulberry at his own home, New Place in Stratford, was by tradition planted by Shakespeare himself; in 1756 a later owner, tired of visitors, had it cut down, and the wood was carved into keepsakes.
    • The black mulberry belonged to the Mediterranean world: grown there since ancient times for the fruit, praised by Roman writers, and planted so thickly in Greece for silk that some derive the name of the Morea — the Peloponnese — from its mulberry trees. It travelled north as a garden fruit tree, slow-growing and very long-lived, the mulberry of old walled gardens.
    • In 1609 King James I of England tried to found an English silk industry to rival France and Italy. He wrote to landowners across the country offering mulberry trees at three farthings each, planted a four-acre royal mulberry garden on ground now under Buckingham Palace and Green Park, and had some ten thousand trees imported. The trees that came were black mulberries. The story usually told is that the king planted the wrong tree. The truth has more give in it: silkworms will eat black mulberry leaves, though they thrive best on white; and the black is by far the hardier tree in a cold, wet England, so it may have been chosen with open eyes. Either way the English silk scheme failed — and the fruit trees stayed. Ancient, gnarled black mulberries in old English gardens, some planted in that era, are its living legacy.
    • North America already had the red mulberry, and its peoples ate the fruit and, in places, wove the inner bark into cloth. The colonists wanted the white one, for silk: Virginia's assembly passed laws in the 1600s requiring settlers to plant mulberry trees, and in the 1730s Georgia's trustees required plantings and shipped small lots of Georgia raw silk to London. Silk stayed a cottage craft — Connecticut became the young republic's silk centre, with the first American silk mill at Mansfield in 1810 — but the tree-planting habit it started never left.
    • Then came the bubble. In the 1830s a fast-growing Chinese mulberry, Morus multicaulis, was promoted as a silkworm feed that could be cut again and again for leaves, and its trees became a speculation: one tree bought for $25 in Massachusetts was sold for $50 in Connecticut, and its new owner refused $450 for a quarter share of it. After the financial Panic of 1837 the price of the trees collapsed — from $1.25 apiece to a few cents within a year — and a killing winter in 1840–41 and blight in 1844 finished the orchards. Farmers tore the trees out and the "multicaulis fever" became a byword for a swindle. The white mulberry escaped anyway: bird-sown from all that planting, it naturalised along fencerows and woodland edges across the continent, where it grows still.
    • In China the whole tree was a medicine chest for well over a thousand years, and those uses are history, told here as history: the leaf was used for fevers and coughs, the root bark — sang bai pi, "mulberry white bark" — for coughs and laboured breathing, the twigs for aching joints, and the fruit to nourish the body and, the medicine books said, darken grey hair. Persian and Indian medicine used the fruit and leaf in their own ways, and in China and Japan the leaf was drunk as a tea, including against sugar sickness — the tradition standing behind the modern leaf-extract studies told in Health Benefits.
    • One name to keep separate, in one line: the paper mulberry is a different tree, Broussonetia papyrifera — a cousin in the same family, the bark-cloth and paper tree of Asia and the Pacific. It is not a true mulberry and bears nothing like this fruit.
    • The nutrition figures are USDA's, measured on the black mulberry. Per 100 g of raw fruit: 43 kcal, carbohydrate 9.8 g, sugars 8.1 g, fibre 1.7 g, protein 1.44 g. The standouts are vitamin C at 36.4 mg — about 40% of the daily value — and iron at 1.85 mg, about 10% of the daily value and unusually high for a fruit, with potassium (194 mg), calcium (39 mg) and a little vitamin K besides. Serving honesty: mulberries are eaten by the handful under the tree, and a full cup (140 g) gives about 51 mg of vitamin C. Dried white mulberries, the form in most shops, concentrate everything including the sugar — they are a sweet dried fruit, closer to raisins than to a health food, and this page treats them that way.
    • The iron and the vitamin C arrive in the same fruit, and that pairing is genuinely useful: vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods eaten at the same meal, and here the fruit brings both. That is ordinary nutrition, stated at its size — a good fruit, not a treatment for anything.
    • Now the blood-sugar story, told at its exact strength, because it is the claim this tree is famous for and it is usually told wrong. The compound behind it is called DNJ (1-deoxynojirimycin), and it lives in the leaf — above all the white mulberry's leaf — not in any useful amount in the fruit. DNJ blocks some of the gut's tools for splitting sugars and starches (enzymes called alpha-glucosidases), so sugar from a meal enters the blood more slowly. What has actually been tested in people is a standardised leaf extract, not the tree as anyone eats it. In the best-known early trial, healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes drank 75 g of sugar water with or without a gram of leaf extract: the rise in blood sugar over the next two hours was about a quarter to a third smaller with the extract — and more undigested sugar reached the lower gut, the trade-off of the method (Mudra et al. 2007). In a later double-blind trial, 37 healthy adults took a branded leaf extract with a starch drink and their blood-sugar rise was 14–22% smaller (Lown et al. 2017). A pooled analysis of 12 small trials, 615 people in all, found small average falls in fasting blood sugar and HbA1c over weeks of leaf or leaf extract (Cui et al. 2023). The fences, plainly: these were short, small trials, several of them funded or co-authored by the maker of the extract; a cup of leaf tea has never been shown to deliver a tested dose; and no trial shows that eating the fruit lowers blood sugar — the fruit itself carries 8.1 g of sugar in every 100 g. Mulberries are not a diabetes treatment, and leaf products are not a substitute for diabetes medicine. Anyone who takes medicine for blood sugar should talk to their clinician before using mulberry leaf products at all, since the leaf's effect could add to the medicine's.
    • The dark fruit's colour comes from anthocyanins — plant pigments that are studied in laboratories for all kinds of effects — and the fruit carries a little resveratrol, the red-wine compound. Both are present in small amounts, and no human trial shows a benefit from eating mulberries for either. The "superfood" claims built on them are dropped here, in this sentence, the way this library drops them everywhere.
    • Cautions, plainly: eat mulberries ripe. The unripe fruit and the tree's milky sap can upset the stomach. And ripe dark fruit stains — hands, clothes, paths, washing on the line. That is not a warning so much as the tree's signature; gardeners plan around it below.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring; give them room — 15–30 ft (5–9 m) from other trees by species and size — and keep them well away from paths, drives, patios and washing lines, because the fallen fruit stains everything under the tree for weeks
    • Sun: Full sun for fruit
    • Soil: Mulberries are famously unfussy — almost any soil that drains will do, including poor and alkaline ground
    • Environment: White and red mulberries are hardy to USDA zone 4; the black is the tender one, zone 5 and warmer, and in cool districts it wants the sunniest, most sheltered spot you have — it will grow, but it fruits late and lightly where summers are short
    • Planter or ground: Ground: white — fast, tough, 30–50 ft (9–15 m), fruit within a few years of planting; black — slow, spreading, 20–30 ft (6–9 m), a tree you plant for your grandchildren as much as yourself, and the best fruit; red — a woodland tree for a shady edge, grown as much for the tree itself as the crop
    • Water: Water young trees regularly while they establish; once settled they stand drought well
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens unevenly — one branch carries white, red and black fruit at once — and ripe fruit lets go at a touch: spread an old sheet under the tree and shake the branches; the ripe fruit falls, the unripe stays. White and red ripen from late spring into early summer; black from midsummer on; ‘Illinois Everbearing’ straggles across the whole season. Eat within a day or two, or cook, dry or freeze the same day

    Garden notes

    • Male and female: most mulberries are one or the other — male trees make pollen and no fruit; female trees make the fruit, and a lone female fruits without any male nearby, the fruit simply being seedless. Nurseries sell named female or self-fertile forms for fruit, and male clones where only shade is wanted. Know which you are buying.
    • Pruning: prune in the depths of winter, while the tree is fully dormant — mulberries bleed sap heavily if cut once the sap rises in spring. Young trees need shaping; an old black mulberry needs almost none and resents hard cutting. Leave veterans alone.
    • The honest problems, stated plainly. The fruit stains — plan the planting place around it. The tree self-seeds: white mulberry seedlings spring up in every fence line and flower bed, and pulling them is a yearly job. And in North America the white mulberry crosses freely with the native red, and the hybrids outgrow the pure reds — red mulberry is endangered in Canada largely for this reason. A gardener in red-mulberry country who wants to help can plant a red or a named hybrid, and pull white seedlings near wild woods.
    • Finally, the pollen: male mulberries shed clouds of it in spring, and mulberry pollen is among the worst hay-fever offenders known. Several desert cities — Albuquerque since 1994, and Las Vegas, El Paso and Tucson as well — ban planting mulberries altogether for this reason. Check your local rules before planting in the Southwest, and plant a female if hay fever lives in your house.
