    Black Currant

    Ribes nigrum

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    FruitLeafSeedBud

    The most intensely flavoured berry in this library, and the richest in vitamin C by a wide margin. The black currant is a small, glossy, near-black berry that hangs in dangling strings — called strigs — from a thornless northern bush. Raw, it is tart, musky and resinous, too much for most people straight off the bush; cooked, juiced or made into the French liqueur cassis, it is one of the great fruit flavours of the cold countries. It also carries the strangest history of any berry here: for much of the 1900s it was against the law to grow it in the United States.

    Varieties

    • 'Ben Lomond' — the first of Scotland's Ben varieties, released in 1975 from the Scottish Crop Research Institute at Invergowrie and named, like all the Bens, for a Scottish mountain. Bred for cold springs and even ripening, it crops heavily with the full, traditional black currant flavour, and it became the commercial standard — the variety behind much of the world's juice.
    • 'Ben Connan' — a later Ben, with some of the largest berries of any variety, on a compact bush; early and heavy-cropping, a favourite where it is grown.
    • 'Ben Hope' — the Ben bred to answer the bush's worst enemy: it resists the black currant gall mite, the tiny pest whose swollen "big buds" spread reversion disease, the virus that slowly ends a bush's cropping life.
    • 'Ben Sarek' — the small-garden Ben: a naturally compact bush, about 3 ft (1 m) tall, with good mildew resistance and full-sized fruit.
    • 'Titania' — a tall, vigorous Swedish variety, released around 1980. Its rust resistance descends from Canada's 'Consort', a grandparent, and with mildew resistance and large crops besides, it is one of the safest plantings for North America.
    • 'Consort' — the variety that changed the law's facts. Released at Ottawa in 1952, it was bred from the Siberian Ribes ussuriense, which cannot carry white pine blister rust, crossed with an ordinary black currant — so 'Consort', and its sister releases 'Coronet' and 'Crusader', are immune to the rust. Its fruit is smaller and its flavour strong and old-fashioned, but where state rules still restrict black currants, the immune varieties are the ones allowed.
    • 'Noir de Bourgogne' — the old French variety of the Dijon cassis fields: small berries of exceptional scent and intensity, grown for the liqueur rather than the table, and written into the rules of Cassis de Bourgogne to this day. 'Blackdown', its usual partner in the maceration tanks, is the rounder, sweeter half of the classic blend.
    • Behind all of them: red and white currants are a different species (Ribes rubrum), cousins rather than varieties of this one, and the gooseberry shares the black currant's genus — its own entry sits beside this one in the family section.

    Around the World

    France — cassis country. Dijon and Burgundy turn the harvest into crème de cassis for the kir and the kir royale, and the berry flavours sorbets, coulis and pâtisserie across the country; the bushes traditionally grew at the ends of the vineyard rows, a second crop from the wine land.
    Britain — the Ribena generation's fruit. Most of the British crop is grown for juice; at the table it is jam, cordial, and the black currant layer of summer pudding, and its flavour is the country's default for anything purple.
    Russia — smorodina is a garden institution: bushes behind every dacha fence, five-minute jam (pyatiminutka) made by the potful, fruit drinks and kissel, and the leaves going into pickle crocks and teapots as a matter of course.
    Poland — the quiet giant: Poland grows more black currants than any other country in the world, most of them frozen or turned into juice concentrate for export — a large share of the world's black currant products begins in a Polish field.
    Scandinavia — svartvinbär in Sweden, mustaherukka in Finland: the bush is at home in the short northern summer, and the berries are made into saft, the strong cordial diluted at every table, and into fruit soups and winter drinks.
    New Zealand — the modern research home of the fruit: Canterbury growers and scientists made black currants a studied crop there, and much of the recent extract and supplement work begins with New Zealand fruit.
    North America — the comeback. Since the bans fell, small farms in New York, the Pacific Northwest and the Northeast have planted the bush again, and craft makers are producing American cassis for the first time in a century — a flavour the continent is relearning.

    Where It Comes From

    • The black currant is native across the cool middle of the world — central and northern Europe and northern Asia, east to Siberia and the foothills of the Himalayas. Wild, it grows where the ground stays damp: stream banks, wet woodland edges, alder thickets and hedgerows. It is a plant of cold winters and mild summers, and everything in its later history follows from that.
    • One name trap is worth clearing at the start. The little dried "currants" sold for baking — Zante currants — are not this fruit at all; they are tiny dried grapes that borrowed the name because of their size. The black currant is a true berry on a bush, kin to the gooseberry, and no relation to the grape.
    • The first cultivation on record is Russian: by the standard account, monastery gardens were growing black currants in the 1000s, and the bush became a fixture of Russian gardens and village plots, where it stays beloved — smorodina — to this day. Western Europe took it up later; it was in gardens there by the late 1500s, and the English herbals of the 1600s knew it well.
    • Those herbals gave the berry a nickname that tells its oldest medical story: quinsy berries. Quinsy was a severe, swollen sore throat, and black currant juice and syrup were the household gargle and soother for it — a use country practice kept for centuries, and the reason a bottle of black currant syrup lived in so many medicine cupboards. Those uses are history, told here as history; what the studies actually support is in Health Benefits.
    • The leaf had its own parallel career. Across Europe, black currant leaf tea was the traditional drink for making the body pass more water and for easing rheumatic aches and gout. That tradition is still on the books: Europe's medicines agency (the EMA) keeps an official monograph for the leaf as a traditional remedy — for minor joint pain, and to increase urine to flush the urinary tract — while stating plainly that no studies in patients have been done. It is a record of long use, not a proof, and this page files it exactly there.
    • The leaf also worked in the kitchen. In Russia, fresh black currant leaves went into the pickle crock with cucumbers for their scent, and were dried for tea; the winter buds, intensely aromatic, were gathered for flavouring and for perfumery, where cassis bud remains a prized material.
    • English settlers carried the bush to the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1629, and through the 1800s it was an ordinary American garden fruit — by 1899 the United States had nearly 7,000 acres of currants and gooseberries. Then came the disease that undid it.
    • White pine blister rust is a fungus that cannot complete its life without two hosts: a five-needle pine and a Ribes bush. On the currant it does little harm; on the pine it can kill the tree. Of all the Ribes, the black currant is the most susceptible — the best host the fungus has. With the white pine timber industry at stake, the federal government banned the cultivation, sale and transport of black currants in 1911, and funded eradication: government crews, and in the 1930s thousands of Civilian Conservation Corps workers, spent years spraying and uprooting currant and gooseberry bushes across the country.
    • The science softened before the law did. It became clear the rust threatens pines mainly where the two hosts grow close together in damp conditions, and plant breeders answered with currants that cannot carry the rust at all — Canada's 'Consort' of 1952, bred from a Siberian species, heads that line. The federal ban was lifted in 1966 and the question handed to the states. Most states let go over the following decades; New York, once the centre of American growing, lifted its ban only in 2003, after a grower's long campaign. A handful of states still ban or restrict the bush today, which is why the garden section below tells American readers to check their state rules.
    • France gave the fruit its most famous form. In 1841, in Dijon, Auguste-Denis Lagoute made the first crème de cassis — black currants steeped in spirit and sweetened into a thick, dark liqueur, from the bushes that grew at the ends of Burgundy's vineyard rows. A century later Dijon's mayor, Canon Félix Kir, popularised a splash of cassis in the local white wine, and the drink took his name: the kir.
    • Britain gave it its other famous form. In 1938 the Bristol firm H. W. Carter launched Ribena, a black currant syrup developed from research by Dr Vernon Charley of the University of Bristol, who had found just how much vitamin C the fruit holds. When war cut off oranges, the government encouraged black currant growing, bought nearly the whole crop, and from 1941 gave black currant syrup free to young children under the Vitamin Welfare Scheme. A generation of British children grew up on the taste — which is why black currant, not grape or cherry, is Britain's default purple flavour to this day.

    Craft

    • The winter buds are a perfumery treasure. Gathered in winter, mostly in Burgundy and the Loire country in France, they are soaked in solvent to draw out their scent — about 30 kg of buds make just 1 kg of the dark, intense extract called cassis bud absolute. Perfumers have used it in fine fragrance since the 1960s and 1970s, and a very little goes a long way.
    • Fresh raw black currant, per 100 g: 63 kcal, carbohydrate 15.4 g, protein 1.4 g — and the headline number of this whole library: vitamin C 181 mg, about twice the full daily value, roughly three times what oranges carry, weight for weight. Behind it: potassium 322 mg, iron 1.54 mg, vitamin E 1.0 mg, calcium 55 mg, and vitamin A 230 IU. The honest serving note, the same one this page keeps for every fruit: 100 g is a good handful of a very tart berry, and most people meet black currant cooked with sugar, as jam, or diluted as cordial and juice — those forms carry added sugar, and this page does not borrow the fresh berry's credit for them. What can be said for the berry is that its vitamin C held up well enough in syrup to carry a wartime children's scheme; that is history's evidence, and it is in the history above.
    • The near-black skin is coloured by anthocyanins — the same family of pigments as in blueberries, here in stronger kinds: mostly delphinidin and cyanidin joined to a sugar called rutinose. Pigments are chemistry, not benefits, and this page treats them that way: they are simply what the eye studies below actually tested.
    • The eyes are where the human evidence sits, and it is real but small, and it tested concentrated anthocyanin extracts, not bowls of berries. In one small double-blind crossover trial, healthy volunteers taking black currant anthocyanins adjusted to the dark better and had less of the temporary focusing shift that screen work causes than on placebo. In one two-year trial — 38 patients with open-angle glaucoma, all on their normal pressure-lowering drops — 50 mg a day of black currant anthocyanins went with slower worsening of the visual field than placebo, and with better blood flow at the optic nerve; eye pressure itself did not change. That is the record at its true strength: two small trial programmes, promising, unproven at scale, and no substitute for glaucoma treatment. Nobody's drops should ever be swapped for currants.
    • Circulation claims rest on smaller ground still: a few short studies, mostly from the same Japanese research group, found black currant anthocyanin drinks increased blood flow in the forearms and shoulders and eased muscle fatigue after typing work. Small numbers, short periods, supplement doses — a hint, not a finding, and this page claims no more.
    • The seed is a separate story. Pressed, the tiny seeds give an oil that is about 15–20% gamma-linolenic acid — GLA, an omega-6 fat the body turns into inflammation-calming compounds — with some omega-3 fat besides, a rare combination. The oil has been tested: in one small six-month trial (34 people with rheumatoid arthritis, about 10 g of the oil a day), joint tenderness improved significantly against placebo. For eczema, GLA oils as a group have been tested more and found wanting — the balance of the evidence is that they do not help. So the seed oil's record, stated plainly: one small positive trial for joints, a negative record for skin, and in both cases a supplement — not something eating the fruit provides in any amount.
    • And the claims that are simply not here: black currant does not detox anything, has not been shown to prevent cancer, lower blood pressure or slim anyone, and its vitamin C — a genuine nutrient fact — is not a tested cold cure. The sore-throat syrup of the old herbals sits in the history, where the evidence leaves it.
    • Cautions, plainly: the fruit in food amounts is safe for most people. The seed oil in trials caused occasional mild stomach upset and headache; like other GLA oils it is a supplement to check against regular medicines before taking. The leaf teas of tradition are a separate matter from the fruit and are told as history on this page, not recommended as treatment.
    • When to plant: Set bare-root bushes in autumn or early spring while dormant, and plant them an inch or two deeper than they grew in the nursery — the buried stem throws up the new shoots the bush fruits on; space bushes 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) apart
    • Sun: Full sun where summers are cool; a little afternoon shade where they are hot
    • Soil: Rich soil that holds moisture without drowning — deep, fertile, well-drained, about pH 6–6.5 — and a thick mulch every year, because its roots run shallow and like to stay cool and damp
    • Environment: Cold is a requirement, not a hardship: roughly 800 to 1,500 hours of cold between freezing and about 45 °F (7 °C) before the buds will break and flower properly — about USDA zones 3–7 (into zone 8 where summers stay cool); dormant, it shrugs off −40 °F (−40 °C), but it flowers early, so plant it out of frost pockets, where cold air drains away
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a deciduous, thornless, multi-stemmed shrub, 3–6 ft (1–1.8 m) tall and about as wide, sending up stems from the base; black currants are self-fertile — one bush fruits on its own — though bees working the flowers make for fuller strigs
    • Water: This is a hungry, thirsty bush by berry standards: a yearly mulch of compost or well-rotted manure, and steady water while the fruit is swelling, are most of its care; dry fruiting wood and drought give small, dropping berries
    • When to pick: The fruit ripens in July in the northern hemisphere, the top berries of a strig colouring first and the string finishing over about two weeks; berries sweeten for a few days after they turn black, so pick whole strigs when the last berries have blackened, strip them with a fork over a bowl — the fruit freezes perfectly, exactly as picked

    Garden notes

    • Pruning is the one skill, and it follows from how the bush fruits: the best crops come on one- and two-year-old wood. Each winter, cut out about a third of the oldest, darkest stems at ground level, and take out anything weak or crossing, leaving eight to twelve strong stems of mixed ages. Done yearly, the bush renews itself forever; left undone, it fades into old wood and small fruit.
    • Troubles, honestly: the gall mite — invisible, living in the buds, which swell round and fail (“big bud”) — spreads reversion disease, the slow end of many old bushes; resistant varieties like ‘Ben Hope’ are the answer, and swollen buds are picked off and burned where they appear. Powdery mildew whites the leaves of susceptible varieties; aphids curl the shoot tips; birds take ripe fruit unless it is netted.
    • And the rust: the bush itself is barely harmed by white pine blister rust, but where five-needle pines grow and state or provincial rules restrict Ribes, plant only the immune varieties — ‘Consort’, ‘Coronet’, ‘Crusader’, ‘Titania’ — and check the local law first. The rule exists to protect the pines, and it is still on the books in a few states.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: currants, European black, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Nakaishi et al. (2000) — effects of black currant anthocyanosides on dark adaptation and screen-work eye strain in healthy volunteers, Alternative Medicine Review
    • Ohguro et al. (2012) — two-year randomised, placebo-controlled trial of black currant anthocyanins on visual field in glaucoma, Ophthalmologica
    • Leventhal et al. (1994) — treatment of rheumatoid arthritis with black currant seed oil, British Journal of Rheumatology
    • European Medicines Agency (2010) — Community herbal monograph on Ribes nigrum L., folium — the leaf's traditional uses, and the absence of patient studies
    • Bratsch & Williams (2009), via Ohio State University — Specialty Crop Profile: Ribes (currants and gooseberries) — the rust, the bans and the state rules
    • Lejay Lagoute, Dijon — the house history of crème de cassis: Lagoute, 1841, and the kir
    • Ribena / Suntory (2024) — Our Story: Dr Vernon Charley, 1938, and the wartime children's syrup

    Gooseberry

    Ribes uva-crispa

    Culinary

    Digestive HealthImmune Health

    FreshCooked

    Fruit

    A small, tart berry on a fiercely thorny bush, and for two hundred years the most competed-over fruit in Britain. Gooseberries live two lives: picked hard and green in late spring, they are a sour cooking fruit for sauces, pies and jam; left to ripen in summer, the dessert kinds turn sweet enough to eat from the bush. The berries come green, yellow, white and red, smooth or softly hairy, and in Britain they are still called goosegogs in the garden. One name to keep separate: the Indian gooseberry, or amla, is a different fruit from a different tree, and none of its story belongs to this plant.

    Varieties

    • 'Roaring Lion' — a red giant of the show era, dating to about 1805. A 'Roaring Lion' berry took first prize at a Nottingham show in 1819 at just under 20 pennyweights, about 30 grams — a monster for its day, and about half what the record weighs now. It stands here for the hundreds of big show varieties the clubs bred, most of them now lost.
    • 'Leveller' — the classic large dessert berry of the Victorian shows: smooth, green-yellow fruit of great size and good flavour, as happy in a pie as on the show bench. Still grown and still a byword for a big gooseberry.
    • 'Careless' — the standard green cooking gooseberry since the mid-1800s: pale green-white berries, heavy crops, reliable in ordinary gardens. If a recipe simply says gooseberries, this is the kind it means — picked green and sour for pies, sauces and jam.
    • 'Whinham's Industry' — a red variety raised in Northumberland in 1835 and named for its raiser, Robert Whinham. Hardy, heavy-cropping and tolerant of shade and poor spots where other kinds sulk; its berries cook well and ripen to a dark, sweet red.
    • 'Whitesmith' — an old white-fruited dessert kind: smooth, pale, almost translucent berries, early and sweet eaten ripe from the bush.
    • 'Invicta' — the modern answer to mildew, raised at East Malling in Kent: a very vigorous bush with some resistance to American gooseberry mildew, bearing heavy crops of pale green berries that cook well and ripen sweet. The variety that brought gooseberries back into ordinary gardens.
    • 'Hinnonmäki Red' — a Finnish-bred variety with mildew resistance in its parentage: medium red berries with a genuinely sweet flavour ripe, on a hardy bush. Finland's breeding programme produced a family of these — red, yellow and green — built for short northern summers.
    • 'Pixwell' — the American answer: released in North Dakota in 1932, bred from the wild American gooseberries. Nearly thornless, mildew-resistant, with pink-red fruit when ripe — the gooseberry for gardens where the European kinds struggled, and easier picking than any of them.

    Around the World

    Britain — the gooseberry's home stage: the club shows of Yorkshire and Cheshire, gooseberry fool (the crushed fruit folded through cream, in print by 1747), crumbles, pies and jam, and the first green berries of the year cooked as a rite of late spring. The traditional sauce went with rich food — roast goose and pork — the sharpness cutting the fat.
    France — the mackerel currant: green gooseberries cooked into a sharp sauce for grilled mackerel, a pairing old enough to name the plant. The fruit is groseille à maquereau; sweet ripe dessert gooseberries never took hold in France the way they did in Britain.
    Germany and Austria — the Stachelbeere, the "prickle berry": baked into cakes and the classic gooseberry meringue torte, made into compotes and preserves, and grown in cottage gardens across the German-speaking lands.
    Scandinavia — gooseberries suit the short, cool summer: grown in Finland, Sweden and Norway, eaten ripe in the brief season and preserved against the winter. Finland's Hinnonmäki breeding station gave the fruit some of its hardiest modern varieties.
    Russia and Eastern Europe — gooseberry jam is a classic of the region, above all the green gooseberry jam cooked to a clear emerald — in its most famous form with walnuts, a preserve with a royal reputation — and the berries are bottled and frozen for winter across Russia, Poland and Ukraine.
    North America — the comeback still under way: after the federal ban lifted in 1966 and the states followed, gooseberries returned slowly to American gardens and farmers' markets, mostly the American-bred kinds like 'Pixwell' and 'Poorman'. Many American gardeners have still never tasted one — the lost half-century is the reason.

    Where It Comes From

    • The gooseberry is native to Europe, the Caucasus, northwestern Africa and southwestern Asia, a plant of woods, hedgerows and rocky ground. The classical writers of Greece and Rome never mention it — it is a northern fruit, and its recorded story starts in the north.
    • The first record of it in England is a purchase: in 1276, gooseberry bushes were bought for the Westminster garden of King Edward I, brought from France. For a long time it stayed a minor garden plant, then spread fast in the 1500s — by 1597 the herbalist John Gerard could write that gooseberries grew "in our London gardens and elsewhere in great abundance."
    • Old medicine valued the berry for its sharpness. Its acid juice was held to cool fevers — one of its old English names is feaberry, the fever berry — and the unripe fruit was used in the kitchen the way verjuice was, as a souring for sauces. Those uses are history, told here as history; what the fruit offers as food is in Health Benefits.
    • Then came the craze, and it was a working people's craze. From the 1700s, and above all in the 1800s, amateur growers — many of them mill workers and miners in Lancashire, Cheshire, Yorkshire and the Midlands — formed gooseberry clubs and competed to grow the single heaviest berry. The clubs met in pubs, kept careful registers, and bred hundreds of new varieties chasing weight: the Horticultural Society's London garden held 360 different gooseberry varieties by 1831, and The Gooseberry Growers' Register, the annual record of the shows, listed 171 separate shows in 1845 alone. Growers thinned each branch to a few berries, fed them, and shaded them from sun and rain under little shelters as they swelled.
    • The shows weighed in the old troy units — pennyweights and grains — and the record crept up across two centuries. In 2013 Kelvin Archer of Cheshire grew a berry of 64.49 grams, about the size of a large hen's egg and the first ever past 40 pennyweights. In 2019 Graeme Watson of Yorkshire beat it with a yellow variety called Millennium at 64.56 grams, and he has since weighed in a berry reported at 65.3 grams. Of the hundreds of shows, nine survive: the Egton Bridge Old Gooseberry Society in Yorkshire, founded in 1800 and the oldest of them, still meets on the first Tuesday of August, and eight clubs remain in Cheshire.
    • The same century that made the gooseberry also nearly unmade it, from two directions at once. Around 1900 a fungus native to North America, the American gooseberry mildew, took hold in Europe — it had been reported in Russia a decade earlier, and in 1900 it was found in Ireland — and spread across the continent. The big European dessert varieties had no defence against it: leaves and berries furred white, fruit cracked, and bushes weakened year on year. Commercial gooseberry growing collapsed across Britain and Europe in the early 1900s. The rescue came from the mildew's own home: breeders crossed the European gooseberry with the smaller wild American gooseberries, which had lived with the fungus and resisted it, and the modern mildew-resistant varieties descend from those crosses.
    • In America the gooseberry was caught in a different fight. A fungus called white pine blister rust needs two hosts to live: a five-needle pine, and any Ribes — currant or gooseberry. To protect the white pine timber forests, the United States government restricted Ribes from 1911, banned it federally under the plant quarantine laws, and sent crews out to dig up and destroy currant and gooseberry bushes, wild and planted, for decades. The federal ban was lifted in 1966 and left to the states; most states had lifted theirs by 2003, and a few still restrict Ribes today. The black currant took the worst of that story — it is told on its own page — but the gooseberry was swept up in it, and American growing lost half a century.
    • Even the name is uncertain. Nobody knows where "gooseberry" comes from: the likeliest story is that it is a worn-down form of the Dutch kruisbes, the German Krausbeere or the French groseille. The popular explanation — that the sharp sauce was served with roast goose — may be a reason invented after the word. In France the fruit kept the pairing that stuck: groseillier à maquereau, the mackerel currant, because its sour sauce was eaten with oily mackerel.
    • Raw gooseberries, per 100 g: 44 kcal, carbohydrate 10.2 g, fibre 4.3 g, protein 0.9 g, fat 0.6 g. The fibre figure is the fruit's quiet strength — more fibre, weight for weight, than most berries in this library — and it comes with the skins and seeds, which are eaten with the fruit. Gooseberries are also naturally rich in pectin, the setting agent of jam, which is part of the same fibre story and the reason gooseberry jam sets so willingly.
    • Its vitamin C is honest and middling: 27.7 mg per 100 g, about a third of the daily value. A full serving does better than the per-100 g figure suggests — a cup of berries, about 150 g, carries roughly 42 mg, near half the daily value — because ripe gooseberries are eaten by the bowlful, not by the spoonful. There is a little potassium (198 mg), a little vitamin A, and small amounts of several B vitamins besides. The red and purple varieties carry their colour as anthocyanins, the same family of pigments that colours blueberries; that is a fact about what is in the fruit, stated here as a fact and not as a promise.
    • And the plain truth about research: the gooseberry itself has barely been studied in people. There are no clinical trials of eating gooseberries to point to — no tested effect on blood sugar, blood pressure, joints or anything else. What exists is laboratory work on extracts, which is not the same as eating the fruit, and a great many claims borrowed from the Indian gooseberry, amla, which is a different plant and whose evidence does not transfer. This page makes no claim for the gooseberry beyond its value as a food: tart, high in fibre, with a fair measure of vitamin C.
    • Cautions, plainly: gooseberries in food amounts are safe for nearly everyone. Very unripe berries are sharply sour — that is their cooking purpose, not a danger. The one real hazard of the plant is in the garden, not the kitchen: the thorns are formidable, and picking is glove work.
    • When to plant: Set bushes 4–5 ft (1.2–1.5 m) apart, cordons about 15 in (38 cm) apart along their support; it fruits young — a bush can carry a real crop in its third year
    • Sun: Full sun gives the best ripe fruit, but the gooseberry tolerates part shade better than most fruit — in Britain it was traditionally grown against a north wall — and a little shade is a kindness where summers run hot
    • Soil: Fertile, moist and well drained, slightly acid to neutral; the bush dislikes both drought and standing water, and its roots run shallow, so keep the ground under the bush clear — hoeing damages them
    • Environment: Cold is its friend: one of the hardiest fruits in this library — dormant bushes stand winter cold to about −30 °F (−34 °C), in USDA zones 3–8 — and it needs a proper cold winter to fruit well; heat is its limit — in hot summers the leaves scorch, growth stalls and mildew thrives
    • Planter or ground: Ground, grown as an open bush on a short bare stem, or trained flat as a cordon or fan against a wall or fence, which saves space and makes picking kinder
    • Water: Mulch in spring to hold moisture and keep the roots cool, and water in dry spells while the fruit swells
    • When to pick: In two passes: from late spring, pick the berries hard and green, thinning the crop as you go — the thinnings go to the kitchen for sauce, pie and jam, and the berries left behind grow the larger for it; then in summer, let the rest ripen fully on the bush for eating fresh — a ripe dessert gooseberry gives slightly when gently squeezed and tastes sweet before it tastes sharp; net the bushes as the fruit colours, or the birds will hold their own show

    Garden notes

    • First, what it is: a small deciduous bush, 3–5 ft (0.9–1.5 m) high and as wide, of arching branches thickly set with sharp spines, alone or in twos and threes at the leaf joints. It is long-lived and undemanding once settled.
    • Pruning, in plain words: each winter, keep the centre of the bush open like a cup — take out crossing branches, weak growth and the oldest wood, and shorten the leaders a little. Air moving through the bush is the first defence against mildew, and fruit forms best on wood two and three years old and on the short spurs of older branches. Wear gloves. Every cut is made among thorns.
    • The mildew, honestly: American gooseberry mildew is still the bush’s main disease — a white powdery coat on young leaves and berries that turns brown and felty, cracking the fruit. The garden defences are the resistant varieties (‘Invicta’, ‘Hinnonmäki’, ‘Pixwell’), the open pruned centre, watering at the roots rather than over the leaves, and picking off the first furred tips when they appear. Fruit with the felt rubbed off is still edible, but a badly mildewed crop is a poor one.
    • The other enemy is smaller: gooseberry sawfly caterpillars can strip a bush to bare ribs of leaves in a few days in spring. Check the leaf undersides from April, and pick off the pale green larvae by hand at first sight — a defoliated bush fruits badly the next year. And a note for American gardeners: a few states still restrict Ribes to protect white pines — check the local rule before planting, and plant away from five-needle pines.

    Sources

    • U.S. Department of Agriculture (2019) — FoodData Central, SR Legacy: gooseberries, raw — the nutrition figures
    • Royal Horticultural Society — Fascinating facts: gooseberries — the 1276 record, 360 varieties by 1831, the Growers' Register's 171 shows of 1845, the mackerel name, and the mildew decline and resistant crosses
    • Salmon (1905) — On the present aspect of the epidemic of the American gooseberry mildew in Europe, Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society — the mildew's arrival and spread
    • Egton Bridge Old Gooseberry Society, with show reports in Country Life (2019) — the surviving shows and the record berries: Archer's 64.49 g of 2013 and Watson's 64.56 g of 2019
    • Benedict (1981) — History of White Pine Blister Rust Control, USDA Forest Service — the Ribes restrictions, eradication campaigns and the 1966 lifting
    • Barney & Hummer (2005) — Currants, Gooseberries, and Jostaberries: A Guide for Growers, Marketers, and Researchers in North America — varieties and growing

    Sea Buckthorn

    Hippophae rhamnoides

    Culinary

    Eye HealthImmune Health

    Cooked

    FruitSeedLeaf

    A thorny, silver-leaved shrub carrying dense ropes of orange berries so sour that almost nobody eats them raw by the handful — and so rich in what they hold that peoples across Asia and northern Europe have prized them for well over a thousand years. One berry carries two different oils: one in its seed, one in its flesh, and they are not the same oil. The plant itself is a survivor — it makes its own nitrogen fertiliser in its roots, holds sand dunes and broken riverbanks together, and fruits through winters that kill softer plants.

    Varieties

    • Sea buckthorn is one species with a family of subspecies, and most of what growers call varieties are bred kinds drawn from three of them. The subspecies differ more than varieties of most fruits do — in size, sourness and vitamin C alike.
    • The European coastal kind (subsp. rhamnoides) — the wild plant of the Baltic and North Sea dunes: small, intensely sour berries, very thorny, and among the richest in vitamin C at around 300–400 mg per 100 g. Most German orchard kinds were selected from it.
    • The Siberian kind (subsp. mongolica) — from the Altai Mountains and Siberia: bigger, somewhat sweeter berries on a hardier plant, and the base of Russian breeding. 'Chuyskaya' — sold in North America as 'Star of Altai' — is its best-known kind: earlier and sweeter than most, with vitamin C near 170 mg per 100 g. 'Titan' is another Russian kind, with berries large by sea buckthorn standards — about the size of a large pea — and a milder flavour.
    • The Chinese kind (subsp. sinensis) — the plant of the Loess Plateau plantings: small, sour berries, and the source of the highest vitamin C measurements ever reported for the species. It is planted by the million hectares for soil holding first and fruit second.
    • German orchard kinds — from the Berlin breeding programme begun in 1979: 'Leikora', heavy-cropping with deep orange fruit ripening in September; 'Hergo', the most widely planted kind in German orchards, its fruit picked by machine; 'Askola', vigorous and rich in vitamins; 'Frugana', one of the earliest and less thorny.
    • The males — because the sexes are on separate plants (see In the Garden), growers also plant named males that make no fruit at all: the German 'Pollmix' kinds, bred only to flower at the right time and shed pollen over the females. A variety list for this plant honestly includes plants you will never pick a berry from.

    Around the World

    Russia and Siberia — oblepikha is a household staple: jam, a tart golden juice, and the oil kept as a home remedy for skin and stomach alike. The Altai region is its breeding heartland, and Siberian gardens grow it where apples fail.
    China — shaji juice is a mainstream drink, sold everywhere, and the state planting programmes that carpeted the Loess Plateau made China the centre of the world crop. Berry, oil and leaf tea all have industries behind them.
    Mongolia — sea buckthorn juice, chatsargana, is a beloved national drink, pressed in quantity in Uvs province and served sweetened; the plant is a traditional remedy there as it is in Tibet.
    Tibet and Ladakh — the high-altitude home: berries gathered from wild thickets along the rivers, juiced and dried, a winter store of vitamins where almost no other fruit will grow.
    Germany and the Baltic — the juice, Sanddornsaft, is a northern speciality, sour enough to be sold sweetened or blended; wild bushes are harvested along the coasts, and the bright bushes are part of the autumn dune landscape.
    Finland — the research home of the berry's chemistry: the Turku programme measured what is actually in the fruit and ran the dry-eye trial described above.
    Canada and the northern United States — a new orchard frontier: prairie plantings of Russian and German kinds, grown for juice and oil in climates too cold for most fruit.

    Where It Comes From

    • Sea buckthorn is native in one long band across the cold half of Eurasia: from the Atlantic coasts of Britain, the Netherlands and the Baltic, across Russia and Central Asia to Siberia, Mongolia, northern China and the Himalayas. Its richest ground — where the plant is most varied — is the high country around Tibet and the Himalaya. In the wild it grows where little else will: sea dunes, gravel riverbanks, dry mountain slopes and cold deserts.
    • Its scientific name is a story in itself. Hippophae comes from two Greek words: hippos, horse, and phaos, light or shining. The tradition behind it, repeated since ancient times, is that the Greeks fed the leaves and young shoots to their horses, and the horses' coats came to shine. The name is the plant's oldest testimonial — told here as the tradition it is.
    • The English name is plainer and slightly misleading. It is not a true buckthorn — that is a different plant, Rhamnus, in a different family — and it does not grow in the sea. It is a thorny bush that grows beside the sea, and the name stuck; the Latin ending rhamnoides simply means "looks like buckthorn."
    • In Asia the plant's written record is long and serious. It is written into the rGyud bzhi, the Four Tantras, the founding text of Tibetan medicine, and it held a place in Mongolian medicine too — used above all for the lungs and coughs, for the stomach, and to keep strength up at high altitude. Chinese medicine took it up in the same spirit, for coughs, digestion, blood circulation and pain. In the Indian Himalaya, in Ladakh, it is a home remedy and a food at once, known locally as tsermang. These are records of traditional use, told here as history; what modern studies support is in Health Benefits.
    • The horse tradition travelled with the plant: across Central Asia the leaves and berry leftovers were fed to livestock, and herdsmen from Greece to Mongolia told versions of the same shiny-coat story.
    • The modern chapter opens in Russia. From the 1940s Soviet researchers studied the plant systematically, and breeders in Siberia — working with the big-fruited Siberian subspecies — raised kinds with larger, sweeter berries. The oil went further: it is reported to have been carried in the Soviet space programme, in the cosmonauts' food and as a skin cream meant to guard against radiation. Germany began its own breeding in 1979, selecting orchard kinds from wild stands; Finland built a research programme on the berry's chemistry.
    • China planted it on a scale nobody else attempted. Most of the world's sea buckthorn — well over two million hectares of it, wild and planted — is in China, much of it set out across the eroding Loess Plateau, where its roots hold crumbling soil and its berries give poor hill farms a crop. No other fruit shrub has been asked to do landscape repair as its day job.

    Craft

    • This is a dyer’s plant three times over: a yellow dye from the fruit, a yellow dye from the stems, roots and foliage, and a blackish-brown dye from the young leaves and shoots. The wood is a craft wood too — tough, hard, very durable and fine-grained, used for fine carpentry and turning.
    • First, an honesty note about numbers. The US Department of Agriculture's food database has no full entry for this fruit, so there is no single official table to quote. The figures below come from research analyses and European food tables, and they swing widely — because the plant itself swings widely. What is true of every kind measured: this is a genuinely vitamin-rich berry. What is not true is any single tidy figure printed on a juice carton.
    • Vitamin C is the headline, and it is real — but variable. Measured values run from under 100 mg per 100 g of berries in some kinds to around 300–400 mg in the wild European coastal kind, with bred Russian kinds near 170 mg and the highest Chinese kinds measured far above all of these. Even at the bottom of that range the berry matches an orange; at the top it carries many times more. Ripeness, place and variety move the number more than any processing does, and this page prints the range rather than picking the biggest figure.
    • The deep orange colour is carotenoids — the pigment family that colours carrots — including beta-carotene, which the body can turn into vitamin A. The berries also carry real vitamin E and useful potassium. The juice is sharply acid and low in sugar for a fruit juice; the sourness is mostly malic acid, the acid of apples.
    • One berry, two oils — and the difference matters, because the two are sold side by side and often mixed without the label saying so. The seed oil, pressed from the small dark seeds, is rich in the two essential fats linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3), which together make up about 70% of it, and it carries much of the plant's vitamin E. It has almost none of the famous omega-7. The pulp oil, taken from the orange flesh, is the omega-7 oil: a large share of it — commonly around a third, measured anywhere from about an eighth to over half — is palmitoleic acid, an omega-7 fat that is rare in the plant world, though your own skin and body make it too. The pulp oil also carries the carotenoids, which is why it is deep orange and why it can tint skin orange for a while.
    • Dry eyes — the best single human study. In a Finnish trial (Larmo et al., 2010), 100 people with dry eye symptoms took either 2 g a day of sea buckthorn oil — a mix of the seed and pulp oils — or a dummy oil, for three months over autumn and winter, with neither patients nor researchers knowing who had which. Eighty-six finished. In both groups the tear film grew saltier as the cold season dried the air, but it rose significantly less in the oil group, and the worst redness and burning were somewhat lower. That is one trial, of a supplement oil, with a modest effect — stated at exactly that strength, it is the strongest human result this plant has.
    • Eczema — the trial that did not deliver. In a double-blind trial (Yang et al., 1999), 49 people with atopic eczema took capsules of seed oil, pulp oil or paraffin oil — the dummy — for four months. The skin of the pulp-oil group improved; but so did the skin of the dummy-oil group, by the statistics even more strongly, and the seed-oil group's improvement did not reach significance. The honest reading is that this trial does not show the oils work for eczema, whatever the tradition says, and the increases in omega-7 in the blood did not track with improvement either. This page makes no eczema claim.
    • Burns, wounds and stomach ulcers — a strong tradition, thin human proof. In Russia and China the oil has a long record of hospital use on burns, slow-healing wounds and skin damaged by radiation, and it is still used there; animal studies support the wound use. But careful trials in people are lacking, so on this page that use stays where the evidence puts it: a documented medical tradition, not a tested treatment. The stomach-ulcer work is likewise in rats, not people.
    • Blood fats and the heart: a handful of small human studies of the berries and oils have mostly come out flat or mixed — no clear effect on cholesterol worth claiming. This page makes none.
    • Cautions, plainly: the berries are very acid — a lot at once can upset the stomach, and the acid is not kind to tooth enamel, which is one reason the juice is usually diluted or sweetened. The pulp oil's pigments can leave skin temporarily orange; harmless, but worth knowing before a wedding. The oils may slow blood clotting slightly, so anyone on blood-thinning medicine should ask their clinician before taking them as supplements, and there is not enough safety knowledge for the oils as supplements in pregnancy. The fruit eaten as food — juice, jam, sauce — is food, and is treated as food here.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring: one male for roughly every six to eight females, within wind’s reach — the pollen travels on the wind, not on bees — and set the male on the side the spring wind blows from; only the females carry berries
    • Sun: Full sun, without compromise — it will not fruit in shade and fades under taller trees
    • Soil: Almost any well-drained soil suits it, sand and gravel included; a neutral to slightly acid soil, around pH 6–7, is its comfort. Its roots carry nodules holding Frankia bacteria — microbes that pull nitrogen out of the air and turn it into plant food — so the bush feeds itself and slowly enriches the poor ground around it
    • Environment: One of the hardiest fruit plants in the world — Siberian kinds stand cold near −40 °C — and it shrugs off heat, wind and salt spray that would strip other shrubs
    • Planter or ground: Ground — a deciduous shrub or small tree, usually 2–5 m tall and as wide, with stiff thorns along the branches
    • Water: Drought-tolerant once its roots are down, but water young plants through their first dry summers, and fruit is better with water in a dry spell
    • When to pick: Berries ripen from late August into October: snip short fruiting twigs, freeze them overnight, and knock the hard berries loose over a tray — the berries sit tight against the branch on almost no stalk, their skins burst at a squeeze, and the thorns guard all of it; berries picked after the first frosts are a little less sharp, and hand-harvesting this fruit is measured in hours, not minutes

    Garden notes

    • The first thing to understand is the plant’s love life: sea buckthorn is dioecious — male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Only the females carry berries, and a female alone will never fruit. You cannot tell the sexes apart until the plants flower, at three or four years old, which is why named kinds, grown from cuttings of known plants, are worth their price.
    • The berries ripen from late August into October and, if left, hang on the bare branches deep into winter, which is when the bush looks its best and the birds get their share. Its narrow leaves are silvery-green — silvered with tiny scales that cut water loss.
    • The honest warning: it suckers. New shoots rise from the roots well away from the plant, and an unmown sea buckthorn becomes a thicket — which is the point on a dune and a problem in a small garden. Do not plant it beside a lawn you love unless you are prepared to patrol the edge.

    Sources

    • Larmo et al. (2010) — the dry-eye trial: sea buckthorn oil by mouth slowed the tear film's seasonal drying in 100 people
    • Yang et al. (1999) — seed oil and pulp oil tested against a dummy oil in eczema: the trial behind this page's caution
    • Yang & Kallio (2001) — the fatty acids of the berry's two oils, measured across subspecies — seed oil versus pulp oil
    • Tiitinen et al. (2005) — sugars, acids and vitamin C measured in sea buckthorn berries
    • Suryakumar & Gupta (2011) — review of sea buckthorn in traditional medicine, Tibetan and Chinese records included, and in modern research
    • Li & Beveridge (2003) — Sea Buckthorn: Production and Utilization — growing, harvest and use, the standard production reference
    • Plants For A Future — Hippophae rhamnoides: dyes from fruit, stems and leaves; wood for carpentry and turning

    Schisandra

    Schisandra chinensis

    Culinary

    FreshDried

    Fruit

    A climbing vine from the cold forests of north-east Asia, grown for one remarkable fruit. Its red berries hold five flavours in a single bite — sweet, sour, bitter, pungent and salty — and its Chinese name says exactly that: wu wei zi, "five-flavour fruit." The skin and flesh are sweet and sour; the seed inside is bitter and peppery; chewed whole, the berry finishes faintly salty. For two thousand years it has been one of China's treasured tonic herbs. In the last century it became a showpiece of Soviet science, and in Korea its dried berries still make omija, the five-flavour tea. One warning belongs at the top, because it is the best-proven fact on this page: schisandra changes how the body handles many medicines (see Health Benefits), so anyone on regular prescription medicine should be careful with the concentrated extracts.

    Varieties

    • Schisandra is not a plant of named garden varieties in the West, and this entry invents none. In China and Korea, production plantings are raised from selected seed lines rather than named kinds. What a gardener actually meets is one named selection and two relatives worth knowing apart.
    • 'Eastern Prince' — the one cultivar widely sold. It was bred at the Vladivostok station of Russia's Vavilov Institute and is self-fertile: a single vine carries flowers that can set fruit on their own, which answers the male-and-female problem set out in In the Garden. Buy a plant grown from a cutting of it — seedlings raised from its seed may not keep the self-fertile trait.
    • Southern schisandra (Schisandra sphenanthera) — not a variety but the sister species, the southern fruit of the Chinese herb trade, from the mountains of central and southern China. Its berries are smaller and dry darker. It is an official drug in its own right and the source of the Wuzhi extract behind the interaction studies above.
    • Red-flowered schisandra (Schisandra rubriflora) — a Chinese relative grown purely as an ornamental climber, for deep red flowers quite unlike this plant's pale ones. It has no food or medicine tradition of its own and is listed here only so the names are not confused.

    Around the World

    Korea — omija-cha, the five-flavour tea: dried berries steeped in water — often cold water overnight, because hard boiling drags out harsh bitterness — and sweetened with honey. From the same ruby-pink juice comes omija-hwachae, a chilled summer punch served with slices of pear and a scatter of pine nuts, a drink of banquets and hot days. Berries are also layered with sugar into a syrup, omija-cheong, and made into wine.
    China — wu wei zi is first a medicine: the dried berries go into classic formulas for the chronic cough and as a tonic, and are drunk as a simple tea and steeped into medicinal wines. The trade form is the dried fruit, sun-dried until dark red and wrinkled.
    Russia — limonnik: the hunters' berry of the Far East, eaten fresh in season and made into juice, syrup, kissel — a fruit drink thickened to a soft jelly — and wine. A tea is brewed from the leaves and young stems as well as from the berries, and the pharmacopoeia tincture was the Soviet form of the medicine.
    Japan — gomishi, known through Chinese-style medicine (kampo) as a minor formula ingredient rather than a kitchen flavour.
    The West — schisandra arrived in the 1990s as a supplement, riding the "adaptogen" banner out of the Soviet research, and gardeners in cold countries have taken it up as a handsome, hardy climber that happens to fruit.

    Where It Comes From

    • Schisandra is a forest vine of the cold north: northern China, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East, where it climbs trees at the woodland edge and along streams. Its crushed leaves and stems smell of lemon, which earned it its Russian name, limonnik — "the little lemon plant."
    • The five flavours are the plant's heart, and the old books map them precisely. The Tang-dynasty physician Su Gong, quoted in Li Shizhen's great Compendium of Materia Medica (1596), wrote that the skin and flesh are sweet and sour, the kernel pungent and bitter, and the whole fruit has a salty taste — "so the five flavours are complete in this fruit." In Chinese medicine each flavour was held to find its own organ: sour to the liver, bitter to the heart, sweet to the spleen, pungent to the lungs, salty to the kidneys. A fruit carrying all five was therefore prized as one that could nourish the whole body at once. That is the tradition as it was held, told here as history.
    • The plant stands near the very beginning of the written herb record. The Shennong Bencao Jing — the Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica, compiled in China around the 1st–2nd century CE from older knowledge — lists wu wei zi in its top class, the "superior" herbs thought fit to take over a long life. The old text praises it for adding to the breath and strength of the body, settling coughs and panting, and making up what the body lacks. Through the centuries that followed it stayed a classic: prescribed for long-standing coughs, for night sweats, for wasting and weakness — history, told as history; what modern studies support is in Health Benefits.
    • In Korea the berry is omija — the same three characters, the same five flavours — and it lived a double life there as medicine and as a celebrated drink (see Around the World). The mountain district of Mungyeong became so known for it that the town holds an omija festival each autumn.
    • In the Russian Far East, the Nanai and other hunting peoples of the Amur river country carried the dried berries and seeds on long hunts, eating a handful against hunger, thirst and exhaustion, and they said the berries sharpened their sight in the dark. It was that hunters' record — a berry that kept men going — that drew scientists to the plant.
    • The Soviet chapter is real and large. From the 1940s, Soviet researchers studied the vine systematically. The word "adaptogen" — a substance said to help the body withstand stresses of many kinds without doing it harm — was coined by the pharmacologist Nikolai Lazarev in 1947 and built into a research programme by Israel Brekhman, with schisandra among the first plants put under the idea. By the early 1960s schisandra was an official medicine in the USSR, listed in its national pharmacopoeia, and it remains in the Russian and Chinese pharmacopoeias today. Soviet studies reported better endurance and mental performance in healthy people — but they were run to the standards of their time and place, and most cannot be checked the way a modern trial can. The page keeps them at that strength.
    • Two fruits share this name, and the difference matters. This entry's plant is the northern fruit, bei wu wei zi. Its sister species from central and southern China, Schisandra sphenanthera — the southern fruit, nan wu wei zi — is an official drug in its own right, and the old books already prized the northern above it. Much modern research, including the strongest medicine-interaction studies in Health Benefits, was done on the southern species. Where that is so, this page says so.
    • What is in the berry: a family of plant chemicals called lignans — the schisandrins and gomisins — found in this form almost nowhere else in nature. They are concentrated in the seed, not the flesh, which is why extracts are made from the whole berry, seed and all, and why simply eating the fruit is a weaker thing than taking an extract. There is no nutrition table on this page: no standard food database (the US Department of Agriculture's FoodData Central has no entry for this berry) lists it, and the page prints no figures it cannot stand behind. Schisandra is used by the spoonful — as tea, dried fruit or extract — not eaten by the bowlful; the fresh berry is sharply sour and mouth-drying.
    • The liver — the famous claim, fenced at its true strength. In animals, schisandra lignans protect the liver against chemical injury strongly and consistently: a 2025 review gathered 54 animal studies and they point the same way. In people, the record is far thinner. In 1970s China, schisandra preparations were found to lower a liver enzyme reading (ALT) in people with hepatitis, and chemists built a synthetic drug from schisandrin chemistry — bifendate — that is still used in China alongside hepatitis treatment. But a lower enzyme reading is not the same as a healed liver, and the reading climbs again when the drug stops. Modern trials of the berry itself are small and mixed: a mixture of schisandra extract and sesame (sesamin) lowered liver enzymes over five months in 40 people — a mixture, so the sesame may share the credit — while a 12-week trial of schisandra alone in 28 women found no significant change in liver enzymes. The honest position: genuinely promising in animals, not proven as a liver treatment in people.
    • Strength and tiredness — the best modern human findings, and they are small. In two Korean trials, each lasting 12 weeks and each comparing the extract against dummy capsules, 1 g a day of berry extract increased leg-muscle strength more than the dummy: one in 45 women past the menopause, one in 54 adults over 50. Muscle size did not change in either. Two small trials, one country, an extract rather than the tea — stated at exactly that strength.
    • Menopause — one small trial. Thirty-six women finished a 12-week trial of a schisandra extract; hot flushes, sweating and heart palpitations eased more than with the dummy capsules. One trial, few women: a hint worth more research, not a settled use.
    • Stress and focus — the "adaptogen" claim in its modern dress. The human evidence rests on the Soviet-era studies described above and on mixture products: the best-known, ADAPT-232, blends schisandra with rhodiola and eleutherococcus, so its results on attention cannot be credited to schisandra alone. No strong modern trial has tested schisandra by itself for stress, calm or mental performance. The marketing runs far ahead of the evidence, and this page says so plainly.
    • Safety — the medicine interaction, which is the best-documented effect schisandra has. Its lignans slow down CYP3A4 — one of the body's main systems for clearing medicines — and block a pump called P-glycoprotein that moves drugs out of cells. In human studies, most of them using the southern species' extract (sold in China as Wuzhi capsules) given to transplant patients, blood levels of the anti-rejection drug tacrolimus roughly doubled to tripled, and levels of the sedative midazolam rose too. The two species share the same lignan chemistry, and the standard interaction references carry the warning for schisandra generally: anyone taking regular prescription medicine — transplant drugs, sedatives, and the long list of medicines cleared through CYP3A4 — should talk to their doctor or pharmacist before using schisandra extracts or strong preparations. A cup of omija tea at the table is a much weaker thing than a capsule of extract, but the caution grows with the dose.
    • Other cautions, plainly: schisandra can cause heartburn, stomach ache, loss of appetite, itching or a skin rash in some people. In the Russian record it can stimulate the womb — it was once used to help a stalled labour along — so it is best avoided in pregnancy. The dried berry as food and tea has centuries of ordinary use behind it; it is the concentrated extracts where the care belongs.
    • When to plant: Plant in spring, spacing vines about 4–6 ft (1.2–1.8 m) apart along their support; plant one male for every few females — or plant the self-fertile ‘Eastern Prince’ and have berries from a single vine
    • Sun: It fruits best with sun on its top growth while its roots stay cool, shaded and mulched — a forest-edge plant by nature
    • Soil: Rich, humus-filled soil that holds moisture yet drains — it is unhappy in a bog and unhappy in dust; slightly acid to neutral suits it (about pH 5.5–6.5)
    • Environment: Cold is this plant’s friend: hardy through USDA zones 4–8, it shrugs off winters down to about −30 °F (−34 °C); heat and drought check it more than frost ever will
    • Planter or ground: Ground, on a support it can wrap — a strong trellis, arbor, fence or wires, put up before the vine needs it; on a support it runs 15–25 ft (4.5–7.5 m) in gardens, and longer in the wild
    • Water: Water through dry spells, above all in the first years and while fruit is swelling
    • When to pick: Pick in autumn, when the whole hanging cluster has turned fully red — late August into September in Korea, later further north — and pick promptly, because the birds know the day as well as you do; the berries are dried in shade or gentle heat until dark and wrinkled, and dried, they keep for the year’s teas

    Garden notes

    • Male and female, in plain words: most schisandra vines are one sex or the other. The small, fragrant, cream-to-pale-pink flowers of late spring are male on one plant and female on another. Only female vines make berries, and only if a male flowers near enough for insects to carry pollen between them. A vine grown from seed keeps its sex secret until it first flowers, usually in its third or fourth year, so seed-growers plant several and keep the mix that results.
    • Patience is the price, as with so many cold-country fruits: two or three quiet years while the roots settle, first flowers around year three or four, and useful crops from year four or five. Prune lightly in early spring — shorten the side shoots and clear out tangles before growth starts.
    • From seed: the seed must be fresh, and it needs a long cold spell — about three months chilled and damp — before it will stir. Cuttings and layers are how named plants and known sexes are kept.
